idiom_name: tokio multi-threaded runtime (per-worker I/O drivers with work stealing); mio::Poll for the hand-written pool
implementation_notes: mio exposes exactly the primitives the classic structure needs - Poll reads readiness events from the operating system into Events, Registry registers sources, and Waker allows cross-thread waking of Poll - so a pool could be written by hand over std::thread, Arc<Mutex<...>> and Condvar. The ecosystem answer is a runtime instead: tokio documents its services as an I/O event loop (the driver) plus a scheduler and a timer, and its multi-thread scheduler runs one worker per core with work stealing, so each worker owns its driver and leadership is never rotated. Choose the hand-written pool (mio plus Waker) only to integrate a foreign descriptor set or when the runtime must not live in the process.
pitfalls: Sharing one mio::Poll across threads repeats the pattern's serialisation problem: only one thread may block in poll() for a given registry, and Waker - not a Condvar - is the legal cross-thread wakeup.
Blocking inside a task occupies a worker and its driver, and the cooperative scheduler cannot preempt it; use spawn_blocking for synchronous work.
Detached tasks must own everything they touch: a task holding a borrowed buffer or a handle from a dead connection is the Rust shape of the dangling-completion bug.
A hand-rolled pool must rearm readiness interest after each dispatch, or an edge-triggered event is never delivered again.
